name: Excel V laser

lead: Excel V is a Cutera clinic laser that pairs a green 532-nm wavelength with an infrared 1064-nm wavelength. People use it to reduce facial redness, small visible blood vessels, port-wine stains and brown spots for a clearer, more even face.

Green light is absorbed by blood and pigment, and the 1064-nm light reaches deeper vessels. Heat closes small vessels or breaks up pigment. Studies naming it are small: a prospective study in 5 adults for port-wine stains, a randomised study comparing 532-nm KTP and 595-nm pulsed dye lasers for red surgical scars, and registered studies in rosacea, hand lentigines and poikiloderma of Civatte.

paras: It is done in a clinic, usually in a short series of sessions. The provider selects the wavelength for the target, vessels or pigment. Treated areas may look red or darker for a short period before settling.
Registry entries reviewed do not summarise adverse effects. Vascular lasers in general may cause bruising or pigment change. It is a clinic-only device.

angle.text: Excel V's green and 1064-nm light is absorbed by vessels and pigment, closing small vessels and breaking up spots for less redness and a more even tone. It is used for rosacea, visible vessels and lentigines, and supporting studies are small.

lead: Excel V is a vascular and pigment laser made by Cutera. It combines a 532-nm green laser (KTP-type, frequency-doubled Nd:YAG) with a 1064-nm Nd:YAG, and is used in clinics to reduce facial redness, visible blood vessels, port-wine stains and pigment such as sun spots (lentigines).[1][2]

People seek this kind of laser to even out skin colour: green light is absorbed by haemoglobin and melanin, so heat is delivered to small red vessels or brown spots while surrounding skin is largely spared. The result users and clinicians aim for is a clearer, more uniform complexion, with less visible flushing, thread veins and spots on the face, neck and hands.[3][4]

Clinic treatment with a vascular laser is usually a short series of sessions delivered by a clinician, and the published literature for lasers of this wavelength family covers redness, vessels, pigment and scars.[5][6]

Published studies naming the device are small. A prospective study in 5 adults used a short-pulse 532-nm Nd:YAG (Excel V) for port-wine stains[1], a randomised open-label study compared 532-nm KTP and 595-nm pulsed dye lasers for erythematous surgical scars[5], and registered Cutera studies include rosacea, lentigines on the hands, poikiloderma of Civatte and spider angioma.[7][3][4][8]
infobox: Redness, vessels, port-wine stains, pigment, scars
Micro-lens array (MLA) studied for skin ageing and scars[9][10]

paras: The 532-nm wavelength is absorbed by haemoglobin and melanin, and the 1064-nm wavelength penetrates deeper. Registered Cutera studies list port-wine stain, rosacea, lentigines, spider angioma, scarring, wrinkles and skin ageing.[1][2][7][3][8][9][10]

A prospective, controlled study of five adults reported on short-pulse 532-nm Nd:YAG (Excel V) for port-wine stains, positioned as an option for lesions where pulsed dye laser results vary.[1] A randomised, controlled, open-label comparison of 532-nm KTP and 595-nm pulsed dye laser for erythematous surgical scars is a related study of the same wavelength family, not specific to Excel V.[5]

Registered Cutera studies include: a 24-participant poikiloderma of Civatte study started in 2011;[4] a 24-participant two-arm study on hand lentigines started in 2016;[3] a 22-participant spider angioma study started in 2016;[8] a 17-person 1064-nm non-ablative rejuvenation study for pigment and photoageing;[11] a 20-participant study of Excel V with the Green Genesis and micro-lens array attachment for wrinkles, rosacea and scarring;[9] a 10-participant multicentre study of the micro-lens array for scarring and skin ageing;[10] a 10-participant pilot of multiple passes on port-wine stains (suspended);[2] and a 15-participant rosacea study combining 532-nm KTP and microsecond 1064-nm Nd:YAG started in 2024.[7] Results are not summarised in the registry entries cited here.

The visible problems this type of laser is aimed at include persistent redness and flushing, fine thread veins (telangiectasias) on the cheeks and nose, spider angiomas, brown sun spots on the face and hands, and the mottled red-brown colouring of poikiloderma of Civatte on the neck and chest.[7][3][4][8] Registered studies of the device include several of these exact complaints, as well as scars and skin ageing treated with a micro-lens array attachment.[9][10]

Facial telangiectasias in general are described as often treated with a laser, in which pulsed light heats the vessel so that it closes and is cleared away; Wikipedia adds that destruction of sweat glands is a noted side effect that rises with the number of treatments, and that sclerotherapy is another treatment approach for telangiectasias, mostly discussed for the legs.[12] Which device suits which lesion is a clinical decision that depends on vessel size, depth and skin type.

Selective photothermolysis underlies vascular lasers: a wavelength absorbed by a target (here, oxyhaemoglobin in vessels, or melanin in pigmented spots) heats it while neighbouring tissue absorbs less. Wikipedia's port-wine stain article describes lasers and other light sources as able to destroy the capillaries behind the stain while sparing overlying skin.[6] The shorter pulse widths, large spot sizes and high fluences available on a frequency-doubled Nd:YAG platform were developed for cutaneous vascular lesions, according to the 2013 port-wine stain study.[1] The 1064-nm beam reaches deeper vessels and has also been studied for non-ablative skin rejuvenation in a 17-person single-centre study.[11]

Registry entries listed here do not report results, so effect sizes cannot be given. For port-wine stains in general, Wikipedia reports that in pulsed dye laser trials most people had over 25 percent of the redness reduced after one to three treatments, that up to ten sessions may be needed, and that trial follow-up was only six months.[6] Whether Excel V's 532-nm mode matches or differs from pulsed dye laser outcomes for individual patients is addressed only in small studies such as the 5-adult trial.[1]

Wikipedia reports that after pulsed dye laser treatment of port-wine stains, pain, crusting and blistering can occur in the following two weeks, and that skin colour changes were seen in some people, particularly those with darker skin.[6] Registry entries for Excel V do not list adverse-event outcomes. Treatment is delivered by clinicians in a professional setting.
